why_how.text: Everyone in a passenger vehicle must wear a federally approved safety belt, the driver is responsible for seeing that all passengers are buckled, the only legal exception is a person eighteen or older riding in the back seat, and a medical exception may be issued with proof of the condition.

Wearing a safety belt cuts the chance of injury or death in a collision by forty-five to fifty percent because the belt spreads crash forces over the strongest parts of the body and helps occupants ride down the crash, the lap belt fitting snugly over the lower hips and the shoulder belt worn with it for upper-body protection.
Properly used safety belts keep you from being thrown forward or out of the vehicle and hold you in the proper driving position on bumpy or twisting roads.

A driver transporting a child under eight in a passenger automobile, van or pickup truck not operated for hire must secure the child in a child passenger safety device that meets federal standards while the vehicle moves on a street or highway, but a child under eight who is at least four feet nine inches tall may be protected by a safety belt alone.
The only legal safety belt exception is a person eighteen or older in the back seat, while a child under eight needs a child safety device unless the child is at least four feet nine inches tall.

why_how.text: Keeping the vehicle in proper driving condition is the driver's job, and the common defects that cause crashes are faulty tires, brakes, lights, windshield wipers, defrosters, mufflers and exhaust systems, horns, mirrors and unusable seat belts.

Make sure you are physically and mentally ready to drive, because the most common driver conditions that affect safe operation are fatigue, alcohol, emotional state, and defective eyesight or hearing.

Fatigue from lack of sleep or driving too long dulls the mind and slows reaction time, so a tired driver who is alone should pull off the road and rest, and when other licensed drivers are aboard drivers should change as soon as one becomes tired.
On a long trip take a ten-minute rest break at least every two hours and spend it outside the vehicle, and rolling the window down, turning the radio on or singing can reduce the monotony of driving.
Emotional states such as anger, worry or fear should be brought under control, and the driver should regain self-control before driving.
The long-trip rest rule is a ten-minute break at least every two hours, and the break counts only when spent outside the vehicle.

why_how.text: The vehicle ahead may stop suddenly and without warning, so stay alert, anticipate a sudden stop and keep a safe following distance to avoid a crash.
You have a responsibility to a tailgating driver behind you to signal whenever you change your driving pattern, because what you do affects that driver, especially if you slow down or stop suddenly.

An oncoming driver may cross into your lane because of sleep, drink, distraction, recovering from a drop off the pavement, turning, trying to pass, avoiding a pedestrian or obstacle, or simply while rounding a curve.
A vehicle at an angle to yours is the situation at intersections, driveways and parking lot entrances and exits, so learn the traffic laws and obey the signs and signals that control those places.

Being passed should never be taken as a challenge, because many sideswipe and run-off-the-road crashes result from it, so check the rear view mirror often, know what is going on around you, slow down and keep as close to the right side of the road as possible to make passing easy.

Passing is acceptable when done legally, smoothly, skillfully and with consideration, but it adds wear and fuel consumption and can involve you in a head-on, sideswipe or run-off-the-road crash, exceeding the speed limit to pass is illegal, and if you must speed to pass you probably do not need to pass.

The ten steps to passing safely are to keep a safe following distance, check oncoming traffic, check the traffic behind, signal before the lane change, move to the left lane, accelerate, warn other drivers with the horn or by flashing the lights, signal the lane change back, merge right when the passed vehicle's headlights appear in your rear view mirror, and maintain a safe legal speed.
When another vehicle passes you, slow down and keep right rather than treating it as a challenge, and when you pass, exceeding the speed limit is illegal.
In the ten passing steps the warning to the other driver comes by horn or flashing lights, and the merge back right waits until the passed vehicle's headlights show in your rear view mirror.

why_how.text: Rush hours bring congested traffic and hurried drivers, usually inbound to metropolitan areas between seven and nine in the morning and outbound between four and six in the afternoon, while rush hours in industrial areas follow the changes of work shifts.

Rush-hour traffic is heaviest on weekdays, weekends bring drivers making longer trips and driving longer hours, and summer vacation travel and holiday weekends increase traffic volume along with tired, hurried and drunk drivers.

Rural driving brings slow-moving farm machinery, stray livestock, game animals and motorists at higher speeds, urban driving brings more pedestrians, bicycles, intersections and stop-and-go traffic, and a defensive driver always notes the heavy trucks and buses that complicate passing and slow traffic on hills.

Keep the doors locked and the windows up while driving or parked, avoid hitchhikers however innocent or needy they appear, learn your vehicle's controls and safety equipment, and turn off your wireless communication device or enable its hands-free function before driving.

Lock purses, wallets, luggage and valuables in the trunk or glove compartment, and if you become lost do not study a map on the roadside but drive to a well-lit, populated public place such as a service station or restaurant, locking the vehicle and taking the keys.

Always park in well-lit areas with your keys in hand as you approach, check inside and underneath the vehicle before entering, and if you feel you are being followed drive to a well-lit populated area and call the police, which in most areas means dialing nine one one.
Metropolitan rush hour runs inbound from seven to nine in the morning but outbound from four to six in the afternoon.

narration.text: This lesson covers traffic conditions and personal safety. The handbook sets out these rules. Rush hours bring congested traffic and hurried drivers, usually inbound to metropolitan areas between seven and nine in the morning and outbound between four and six in the afternoon, while rush hours in industrial areas follow the changes of work shifts. Rush-hour traffic is heaviest on weekdays, weekends bring drivers making longer trips and driving longer hours, and summer vacation travel and holiday weekends increase traffic volume along with tired, hurried and drunk drivers. Metropolitan rush hour runs inbound from seven to nine in the morning but outbound from four to six in the afternoon.

The handbook states the following. Rural driving brings slow-moving farm machinery, stray livestock, game animals and motorists at higher speeds, urban driving brings more pedestrians, bicycles, intersections and stop-and-go traffic, and a defensive driver always notes the heavy trucks and buses that complicate passing and slow traffic on hills. Keep the doors locked and the windows up while driving or parked, avoid hitchhikers however innocent or needy they appear, learn your vehicle's controls and safety equipment, and turn off your wireless communication device or enable its hands-free function before driving.

The handbook states the following. Lock purses, wallets, luggage and valuables in the trunk or glove compartment, and if you become lost do not study a map on the roadside but drive to a well-lit, populated public place such as a service station or restaurant, locking the vehicle and taking the keys. Always park in well-lit areas with your keys in hand as you approach, check inside and underneath the vehicle before entering, and if you feel you are being followed drive to a well-lit populated area and call the police, which in most areas means dialing nine one one.
